questions.q: What does the rule "code counts, AI explains" mean in the weekly digest blueprint?
options: The AI step pulls the raw figures from each source and calculates the weekly changes itself
Formulas or a code step calculate every number, and the AI only writes the narrative from that finished table
A code step writes the digest text, and the AI step double-checks that the arithmetic is correct
The AI estimates the trends from raw data, and formulas round its figures before the digest is sent
questions.explain: Language models describe data well but aren't reliable calculators, so formulas compute every total, change and average, and the AI receives a finished table to explain.

questions.q: Your digest's number check flags a figure in this week's narrative that doesn't appear anywhere in the data table. What should the workflow do?
options: Send the digest to the whole team anyway, since most flags are false alarms
Ask the AI to recalculate the figure and replace it automatically before sending
Delete the flagged sentence and deliver the rest of the digest to the team
Send the digest to its owner for a quick look instead of to the whole team
questions.explain: The lesson says that if the check finds numbers that aren't in the table, the digest goes to its owner for a quick look, because a confident, wrong number damages trust fastest.

questions.q: While testing, you remove the "Calls booked" row from the data table. What should a well-built digest do?
options: Say that the calls-booked metric is missing rather than inventing a figure
Estimate calls booked from last week's figure and the four-week average
Leave the metric out silently so the digest stays under 200 words
Stop the workflow and resend last week's digest to the team instead
questions.explain: The prompt tells the AI to use only the numbers provided and to say so if a metric is missing, and the testing checklist checks that the digest reports it missing instead of inventing it.
